cards.claim: For SGD, halving the learning rate is equivalent to doubling the batch size in terms of loss dynamics
cards.conditions: SGD on noisy linear regression; same number of data points processed per phase
cards.effect: Excess risk of base process (double batch, fixed lr) within constant factor of alternative (fixed batch, halved lr)
cards.quote: doubling the batch size can be equivalent to halving the learning rate

cards.claim: For normalized SGD (Adam proxy), lr decay by √2 and batch size doubling are equivalent when variance-dominated (Assumption 2 holds)
cards.conditions: Normalized SGD; variance-dominated regime where noise term dominates expected gradient squared norms; same number of data points per phase
cards.effect: Excess risk equivalence maintained within constant factor when product √(β) held constant
cards.evidence: Corollary 1 extending Theorem 1 to normalized SGD under Assumption 2
cards.quote: For NSGD, informally, Corollary 1 shows that any learning rate cut by a factor of √2 and batch size increase by a factor of 2 are equivalent as long as √(β) is held constant.

cards.claim: Beyond critical batch size (CBS), Assumption 2 fails: variance becomes negligible and lr decay cannot be matched by batch size ramps
cards.conditions: Batch sizes past CBS (~256 for 150M models); Adam/normalized SGD; large batch regime where noise variance ~1/B becomes small
cards.effect: Neither Seesaw nor constant-lr + increasing-batch-size schedules match cosine decay performance; discrepancy increases with batch size
cards.evidence: Section 4.2, Figure 3 empirical results; toy NGD analysis showing need for lr decay when batch-size limit reached
cards.quote: Up to this point, a crucial assumption for the development of our theory and the design of Seesaw has been Assumption 2... past a certain batch size, the additive noise will become small, and thus Assumption 2 will fail... We hypothesise that beyond a certain batch size, it is not possible to match the performance of learning rate decay by any equivalent batch size ramp up for Adam or normalized SGD

cards.claim: Variance term in gradient norms scales inversely with batch size (~1/B)
cards.conditions: Stochastic optimization with additive noise; equation 5 decomposition of expected gradient norms
cards.effect: As batch size increases, variance component shrinks, moving regime from variance-dominated to bias-dominated
cards.evidence: Equation 5 analysis: variance scaling term explicitly shown
cards.quote: where the variance scales down with the batch size

cards.claim: Maximum aggressive batch-size ramp without divergence: (α·√β)^0.5, where α is lr decay factor and β is batch size multiplier
cards.conditions: Step decay scheduler approximating cosine decay; continuous-time limit; NSGD with Assumption 1 and 2
cards.effect: More aggressive schedules (e.g., α=0.5, β=4 giving product 1.414) cause instability and performance degradation
cards.evidence: Lemma 4 theoretical constraint; Figure 2 empirical validation on 150M models at batch sizes 256 and 512
cards.quote: Remark 1. The most aggressive ramp up scheme we can use is given by (α·√β)^0.5. (for a formal argument see Lemma 4)

cards.claim: Critical batch size (CBS) defines the maximum batch size maintaining sample efficiency; beyond CBS, further batch scaling reduces data efficiency
cards.conditions: LLM pretraining; data and model size dependent (e.g., 256 tokens for 150M, 512 for 300M at Chinchilla scale)
cards.effect: At or below CBS: batch ramp (Seesaw) matches cosine decay performance while reducing wall-clock time ~25%. Beyond CBS: performance degradation regardless of lr-batch scaling strategy
cards.evidence: Section 1 Introduction, Section 4 empirical design, Figure 1 results at CBS, Figure 3 failure past CBS
cards.quote: However, beyond a maximum batch size termed as critical batch size (CBS), further scaling reduces sample efficiency and limits gains in training speed.

cards.claim: Under Assumption 2 (variance-dominated regime), normalized SGD reduces to SGD with rescaled learning rate, enabling equivalence extension to Adam-like optimizers
cards.conditions: Variance-dominated regime; Assumption 2 holds; at or below CBS
cards.effect: Simplifies NSGD analysis to SGD case, allowing theoretical equivalence between lr decay and batch ramp to extend from SGD to approximate-Adam case
cards.evidence: Section 3.1 design rationale; Equation 11 reduction; Appendix B analysis
cards.quote: Under Assumption 2, the NSGD process effectively reduces to SGD with a rescaled learning rate (Equation 11), up to constant factors.

cards.claim: Assumption 2 (variance-dominated regime) is a precondition for lr-batch equivalence in adaptive optimizers; it holds when noise variance >> expected gradient norm
cards.conditions: Early-to-mid training; batches at or below CBS; structured loss landscape where additive noise dominates
cards.effect: When Assumption 2 holds: equivalence preserved; when Assumption 2 fails (large batch): theory breaks and batch ramp cannot match lr decay
cards.evidence: Section 3.1 assumption statement; Appendix B justification; Section 4.2 empirical failure demonstration past CBS
cards.quote: To design Seesaw, we assume that the [noise term] dominates the expected gradient squared norms (Assumption 2), and we motivate why this assumption is reasonable in Appendix B. This step reduces (up to constant factors) the NSGD update rule to SGD with a rescaled learning rate
